title: Three-Dimensional Linear Transformations: Basis Vectors, 3x3 Matrices, and Transformation Composition
summary: This short footnote from 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra expands the prior two-dimensional focus into three dimensions. It explains that a 3D linear transformation is fully described by the images of the three standard basis vectors (i-hat, j-hat, k-hat), whose coordinates form the columns of a 3×3 transformation matrix. The video shows how to visualize a 3D transform by tracking how basis vectors move, how to compute the image of an arbitrary vector via matrix-column scaling and summation, and how multiplying two 3×3 matrices corresponds to composing two transformations. It also highlights the practical significance of 3D transforms in fields like computer graphics and robotics, and it briefly points forward to the determinant as the next topic.
topics: images of basis vectors under a 3D transform
construction of a 3x3 matrix from basis coordinates
rotation in 3D (example: 90-degree rotation around the y-axis)
applying a 3x3 matrix to a 3D vector
pre- and post-transformation scaling and addition
vector decomposition with respect to a basis

sections.title: Generalizing 2D transforms to 3D and grid-based visualization
concepts: extending linear transformations to three dimensions
grid in 3D space as a proxy for spatial vectors
sections.description: The video discusses visualizing a 3D linear transformation by smooshing the 3D space (represented as a grid) while keeping grid lines parallel and the origin fixed. It emphasizes that, just as in 2D, every point in space is a proxy for a vector, and the goal is to map input vectors to their outputs under the transformation.

sections.title: Basis vectors in 3D and forming the transformation matrix
concepts: three standard basis vectors: i-hat, j-hat, k-hat
keeping a copy of the original axes in the background
coordinates of the basis vectors become matrix columns
sections.description: The video introduces the 3D basis vectors i-hat, j-hat, and k-hat, and explains that tracking where each of these basis vectors lands under a transform helps describe the entire transformation. It then states that the coordinates of these landed basis vectors are recorded as the columns of a 3×3 matrix, yielding a full description of the transformation with nine numbers.

sections.title: Applying the matrix to a 3D vector
concepts: interpret each coordinate as instructions for scaling the corresponding basis vector
sum the scaled basis vectors to get the transformed vector
pre- and post-transformation invariance of the process
sections.description: To find where a vector (x, y, z) lands, multiply the coordinates by the three columns of the matrix and add the results. The video emphasizes that this scaling-and-adding process is consistent before and after the transformation, mirroring the 2D case.

sections.title: Matrix multiplication as transformation composition
concepts: multiplying two 3×3 matrices corresponds to applying the right-hand transformation first
sections.description: The transcript explains that composing two transformations via matrix multiplication is the same as applying the right-hand matrix’s transformation followed by the left-hand matrix’s transformation, a crucial viewpoint for understanding sequential transformations in 3D.

sections.title: Why 3D matrix multiplication matters and upcoming topics
concepts: importance for computer graphics and robotics
breakdown of complex 3D rotations into simpler components
sections.description: The video notes that 3D matrix multiplication is fundamental in fields like computer graphics and robotics because rotations in 3D can be decomposed into simpler rotations. It also teases determinant as the next topic.

featured_techniques.technique: Describe 3D linear transformations via the images of the standard basis vectors (i-hat, j-hat, k-hat) and form the 3×3 matrix from their coordinates
Construct the 3×3 transformation matrix by recording the coordinates of i-hat, j-hat, and k-hat as its columns
Rotate 3D space by a 90-degree transformation around the y-axis as a concrete example
Compute the image of a 3D vector by multiplying its coordinates with the matrix columns and summing
Interpret matrix multiplication as the composition of two transformations (apply right-hand matrix first, then left-hand)
Recognize the practical relevance of 3D matrix multiplication for graphics and robotics
